before: A type parameter appears in square brackets after the function name. First[T any] permits any element type and returns a T. The compiler can infer T from a typed slice argument.

A generic function still needs ordinary bounds checks. var zero T declares T’s zero value. Returning (zero, false) on an empty slice avoids indexing it; the Boolean tells the caller whether an element existed.
Expected output or behavior: 7 true. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Call First with a string slice and predict the zero value for an empty input. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A generic function uses a type parameter: a name that stands for a type. In `First[T any]`, T can be any type. Go can work out T from the slice passed to First.
The function must still check whether the slice is empty. `var zero T` gives the zero value for the chosen type. Returning zero and false avoids reading a missing first item.
The screen shows `7 true`. T is int, and the first integer exists.
With an empty integer slice, zero is 0. With an empty string slice, zero is empty text. The false flag says no first item existed.
